summary: This document explains how IPv4 and IPv6 coexistence combined with poor IPv6 support in VPN products can make traffic that should go through an encrypted tunnel leak out unprotected on the local network. It discusses the problem and mitigations.

eli5.summary: Imagine a secret tunnel that only covers one of two doors. Some of your messages can sneak out the other door in plain view. This RFC explains why that happens.

questions: why does my vpn leak ipv6 traffic
why does a vpn leak ipv6 traffic
what is a dual stack host
how to stop vpn ipv6 leak
subtitle: How a VPN that ignores IPv6 can let your supposedly protected traffic escape in the clear.

tldr.problem: Many VPN products only handle IPv4, but the hosts running them are dual-stack, so traffic sent over IPv6 never enters the encrypted tunnel.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how IPv4 and IPv6 coexist through DNS, how that lets traffic bypass an IPv6-unaware VPN client, and how an attacker can deliberately trigger it with forged Router Advertisements.
tldr.outcome: The proper fix is VPN clients that handle IPv6; the stopgap is disabling IPv6 on all interfaces. The IESG attached a note saying the document does not describe the general issue well.

today: RFC 7359 is an Informational document and is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC. It carries an IESG Note stating that the IESG does not think blaming IPv6-unaware VPN software is an appropriate characterization, since leakage can come from any unencrypted interface, including split tunnels.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
People often use a VPN on a public, possibly hostile, local network. They assume that everything they send is protected by the tunnel, and sometimes even assume it is then fine to use insecure protocols over it.

This RFC shows that some traffic might not be mapped onto the VPN tunnel and so might be sent in the clear on the local network. Many VPN products support only IPv4, while the hosts they run on are dual-stacked: they support and enable both IPv4 and IPv6 by default.

The document covers Layer 3 VPNs, meaning IPsec-based and SSL/TLS-based tunnels. It excludes SSL/TLS VPN portals, which wrap one application protocol such as HTTP.
sections.eli5: You put your letters in a locked mailbox, but your house has a second, unlocked mailbox too. Some letters end up in the wrong one.

sections.title: How IPv4 and IPv6 Coexist
sections.content:
IPv6 is not backwards-compatible with IPv4. The two are glued together by the Domain Name System (DNS). A site with both protocols has A records (each holding one IPv4 address) and AAAA records (each holding one IPv6 address) under the same name.

A dual-stack client can ask for both and use any of the addresses. Which family it picks varies by implementation, and many hosts prefer IPv6. So the DNS answers usually decide which protocol is used to reach a system.
sections.eli5: A phone book lists two numbers for the same friend, an old style and a new style. Your phone may choose the new one without telling you.

sections.title: Where the Leak Comes From
sections.content:
Many VPN tunnel implementations do not support IPv6, or completely ignore it. After the tunnel is up, the VPN software typically inserts an IPv4 default route so all IPv4 traffic goes over the tunnel instead of the local router.

Packets destined to an IPv6 address are not touched. They go out in the clear through the local IPv6 router. The RFC's reasoning is that on a dual-stack system you cannot secure communication with another system without securing both protocols.

In a legitimate dual-stack network the leak is an accident. If the destination has both A and AAAA records, the host may choose IPv6, and that traffic has neither integrity nor confidentiality protection from source to destination.
sections.eli5: The tunnel only watches the old-style road. If your message takes the new-style road, nobody wraps it up first.

sections.title: Deliberate Leakage Attacks
sections.content:
A local attacker can switch on IPv6 connectivity on the victim by sending forged ICMPv6 Router Advertisement messages. After that, talking to dual-stacked systems can leak as described above.

That only works for dual-stacked destinations. For any destination, the attacker can advertise himself as the local recursive DNS server using the Recursive DNS Server (RDNSS) option in forged Router Advertisements, then spoof DNS answers to become a man in the middle. The RFC notes that some systems prefer IPv6-based DNS servers over IPv4 ones, so the malicious server may win over the one advertised by the VPN server.
sections.eli5: A stranger in the cafe shouts a fake set of directions, and your phone follows them instead of the safe ones.

sections.title: Mitigations
sections.content:
The RFC says that at the time of writing a large number of VPN implementations had not addressed this. Some handle IPv6 only partly and miss attacker routes injected through Router Advertisements with Prefix Information or Route Information Options, or ICMPv6 Redirects.

  • If the client sends all IPv4 traffic to the VPN and lacks IPv6 support, disable IPv6 on all network interfaces. This is only a temporary workaround.
  • If the client supports IPv6, make sure all IPv6 traffic also goes via the VPN. Handling every route-injection vector may be nontrivial.
  • In split-tunnel mode, an unaware client should disable IPv6; an aware one needs administrators to route the correct IPv4 and IPv6 networks into the tunnel.

Networks can use First-Hop Security such as RA-Guard, but a host cannot rely on that on an open network, and popular RA-Guard implementations are known to be vulnerable to evasion. The RFC also warns that an IPv6-only VPN that ignores IPv4 could have the mirror-image problem.
sections.eli5: The best fix is a tunnel that covers both roads. If you cannot get one, closing the new-style road completely keeps messages from sneaking out.
